doc.title: Ray Shiner interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 11, 1998

title: First jazz listening and the Sauter-Finegan audition call
summary: Hearing Benny Rides Again, the call from Kay Finegan, Eddie Sauter hiring him, and the teaching degree that later led to Potsdam.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Well you obviously picked up a succession of instruments along the way. And your own personal taste in music eventually turned to swing—
And jazz. Can you recall the first listening experience with either of those with jazz that registered on you?

Well it’s hard to pin down except I remember specifically hearing Benny Goodman play “Benny Rides Again” a new arrangement by Eddie Sauter, when I was in high school. And when I got the call in Rochester from a woman who identified herself as from the Willard Alexander Agency, it was really Kay Finegan, Bill Finegan’s wife, about auditioning for the Sauter-Finegan Orchestra, of course I was elated beyond expectation to hear that, because that’s the greatest band that ever happened. And I started to rave about Eddie Sauter, didn’t say a word about Finegan.
You didn’t know that you were talking to his wife.

Well of course I had remembered “Benny Rides Again” from 1939, which Eddie wrote for Benny Goodman. And then when I auditioned for the band, I didn’t believe it until I got to New York and saw who was there at the audition, that I was really auditioning for the Sauter-Finegan. Then when Eddie called me three days later and he says, “We’d like to have you on the band,” I started to cry.
And you left school to go do that?
I was out of school by then.
Oh you were, okay. And did you graduate with a teaching degree?
I got a teaching degree because my oboe teacher said it would never hurt my playing.
Oh. Well that’s an astute comment. Right.

Of course he was the solo oboist with the Rochester Philharmonic, and I was extra man with the Philharmonic. He says, “It never hurt me getting my job here,” and he says, “it’s not going to hurt you.” Which, it really paid off, years later I called him up from New York, I says, “I’ve had it with this playing,” I said, “get me a teaching gig.” He says, “There’s an opening at Potsdam.”
Oh no kidding. That’s interesting that that connection, so many years later—
Well he was teaching at Potsdam summers. He turned out to be one of my deepest, closest friends and deepest influence.
